title: Gatev, Goetzmann and Rouwenhorst’s design
objectives: Describe the formation and trading periods of the distance method.

screens.title: Two shares that moved together
screens.prose: Shares A and B moved together for a year. Both start at 1 on day 0. On day 280, early in the second shaded block, A sits well below B.
screens.question: A desk trades the gap between them. What does it do on that day?

options.text: Buy A, the laggard, and sell B, the leader, then wait for them to meet
Buy B and sell A, since B has the momentum
options.why: You bet the gap keeps widening. That is momentum, the opposite trade.

options.text: Buy both, since they usually rise together
options.why: Buying both is a bet on the market, not on the gap.

options.text: Do nothing until the gap closes
options.why: Once the gap has closed, the profit from closing it is gone.

hints.text: The desk expects the gap to close.
Which share has to rise, relative to the other, for the gap to close?
A must catch up with B: own A, owe B.

feedback.correct: Correct. Buy the cheap one, sell the dear one, and wait for convergence.
feedback.generic: Not quite. The trade profits if the gap closes, whichever way the market moves.

byKey.mom: You bet on the gap widening. The pairs trade bets on it closing.

explain.text: On day 280 A is about 0.053 below B in normalised terms. Owning A and owing B gains when the gap shrinks, whatever the market does. Here the lines met again on day 295.

screens.title: A new portfolio every month
screens.prose: Gatev, Goetzmann and Rouwenhorst (2006) form pairs over a year and trade them over the next six months. A new portfolio starts every month, or 21 trading days. Slide through the first six.

state.caption: Portfolio 1: forms on days 0 to 251, trades on days 252 to 377.

Portfolio 2: forms on days 21 to 272, trades on days 273 to 398.
Portfolio 3: forms on days 42 to 293, trades on days 294 to 419.
Portfolio 4: forms on days 63 to 314, trades on days 315 to 440.
Portfolio 5: forms on days 84 to 335, trades on days 336 to 461.
Portfolio 6: forms on days 105 to 356, trades on days 357 to 482.

screens.question: On day 360, how many of these six portfolios are in their trading period?

widget.accept: 6: every portfolio started on days 0 to 105 is trading on day 360

hints.text: Check each portfolio's trading block in turn.
Portfolio 6 trades from day 357. Does day 360 fall inside its block?
Every block from portfolio 1 (days 252 to 377) to portfolio 6 (days 357 to 482) holds day 360.

feedback.correct: Correct. All six trade at once on day 360.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Slide through all six and check whether day 360 sits in each trading block.

byKey.one: You counted only the first portfolio. The later ones are trading too.
byKey.five: Portfolio 6 starts trading on day 357, so day 360 is inside its block too.

explain.text: Each portfolio trades for 126 days and a new one starts every 21 days. 126 / 21 = 6, so from the sixth month on six portfolios are always live. Momentum studies overlap their portfolios in the same way.

canvas.caption: Portfolio 6: forms on days 105 to 356, trades on days 357 to 482.

screens.title: The design in numbers
screens.prose: From the paper's data section, paraphrased: "Each month, every share's total-return index is set to 1 twelve months back. We match each share with its closest partner. The 20 closest pairs, and separately the 5 closest, trade over the next 6 months. A pair opens when the gap exceeds two standard deviations."
screens.question: Fill in the four numbers of the design.

hints.text: Every number is in the quoted passage.
The question asks for months, not trading days.
12 months to form, 6 to trade, 2 standard deviations, 20 and 5 pairs.

feedback.correct: Correct. These four choices are the whole design.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Read each number from the passage, in months.

byKey.days-f: 252 is the formation period in trading days. The table asks for months: 12.
byKey.days-t: 126 is the trading period in trading days. The table asks for months: 6.

explain.text: Formation lasts 12 months and trading 6. Pairs open at 2 standard deviations, in portfolios of the 20 or 5 closest. We call the two blocks the **formation period** and the **trading period**.

screens.title: Which period does each rule use?
screens.prose: Each rule works on one block of days. Formation rules use only the past year. Trading rules act day by day in the next six months.
screens.question: Drag each rule to the period it belongs to.

tokens.text: Scale each path to 1 on its first day
Measure the distance of every pair
Open a pair at a 2 sd gap
Close any open pair on the last day

hints.text: Ask of each rule: does it choose, or does it act?
Choosing pairs and measuring their spread both need the whole past year.
Scaling, distance, selection and the sd belong to formation. Opening and both closes belong to trading.

feedback.correct: Correct. Four rules choose, three act.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Rules that choose or measure use formation days. Rules that act on a day use trading days.

byKey.t4: The sd must be known before trading starts, so it comes from formation days.
byKey.t1: Scaling happens once, on the first formation day.
byKey.t5: Opening acts on a trading day, so it belongs to trading.

explain.text: Everything that chooses or measures is fixed at the end of formation. Trading only reads prices and acts. That split is what makes the backtest honest.

screens.title: Windows in code
screens.prose: Days are counted from 0. Write the two helpers every later screen uses. Ranges are half-open, like Python's `range`, so `(0, 252)` means days 0 to 251. A portfolio is named by its first trading month and trades for `K` months.
screens.question: Complete `cycle_windows` and `live_portfolios`.

widget.how: Submit runs 10 hidden tests: the first cycle, later starts, shorter windows, the first months and a 3-month holding.

hints.text: Trading starts where formation stops.
In month 7 with K = 6, the oldest live portfolio started in month 2.
`return list(range(max(0, month - K + 1), month + 1))`.

feedback.correct: Correct. These two helpers fix the calendar for the whole course.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Trading starts at `day0 + form`. In the first months fewer than K portfolios exist.

explain.text: The half-open ranges slice straight into arrays: `close[f0:f1]` is the formation year. The `max(0, ...)` handles the first months, before six portfolios exist.

screens.title: Which standard deviation?
screens.prose: The spread is A minus B. Its standard deviation over the formation year is 0.0210, so the trigger is ±0.0419. A colleague says the trading-period sd, 0.0300, fits the trading days better.
screens.question: Which sd may the strategy use on a trading day?

options.text: The formation-period sd, fixed before trading starts
The trading-period sd, since it describes the days we trade
options.why: That sd uses prices from days that have not happened yet. It is look-ahead.

options.text: The sd over all twelve years, the most data we have
options.why: Eleven of those years lie in the future of most trades. It is look-ahead.

hints.text: On a trading day, which prices does the desk know?
The trading-period sd needs the last trading day's price.
Only the formation sd is known when trading starts.

feedback.correct: Correct. The threshold is fixed from formation data.
feedback.generic: Not quite. A rule may only use prices known on the day it acts.

byKey.trade: You measured the threshold on the days you then trade. On the first trading day those prices do not exist yet.

explain.text: On the first trading day the desk knows only the formation prices. A threshold computed on trading prices sees the future, and it flatters the backtest. The paper fixes the sd at the end of formation.

screens.title: A share that stops trading
screens.prose: Edge case. A pair is open when share B is taken over on day 300 of the cycle. B's last price is on day 299. The paper has a rule for this.
screens.question: What happens to the open pair?

options.text: Close both legs at B's last price on day 299
Drop the pair from the results
options.why: Dropping it hides a real outcome. The paper keeps every nominated pair.

options.text: Hold B at zero until day 377
options.why: B was bought out for cash, not wiped out. Its last price is what holders received.

options.text: Replace B with its next-closest partner
options.why: The replacement was never in the formation choice. It would be a new trade.

hints.text: The pair must be closed somehow.
What did holders of B actually receive?
The paper closes the pair at the last available price.

feedback.correct: Correct. The pair closes at the last price.
feedback.generic: Not quite. The paper closes the pair at B's last price and keeps the result.

byKey.drop: Dropping it removes a trade that happened. That biases the results.

explain.text: The pair closes at the last price, and its gain or loss counts. Our seeded panel has no delistings, so this rule never fires here. A real replication must code it.

screens.title: The calendar of a cycle
screens.prose:
For a cycle that starts on day $d$:
$$\text{formation} = [d,\ d + 252), \qquad \text{trading} = [d + 252,\ d + 378)$$
A new cycle starts every 21 days. Since $126 / 21 = 6$, six portfolios trade at once.
screens.question: A cycle starts on day 1,134. On which day does its trading period begin?

hints.text: Trading begins when formation ends.
Formation lasts 252 days.

feedback.correct: Correct. Trading runs from day 1,386 up to day 1,512.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Add the 252 formation days to the start.

byKey.end: 1,512 is where trading stops, 378 days after the start.
byKey.trade: You added 126, the trading length. Formation comes first and lasts 252 days.

explain.text: Trading starts at 1,134 + 252 = 1,386 and runs up to day 1,512. Day 1,512 will matter later in the course.

screens.title: The desk's morning screen
screens.prose: A statistical-arbitrage desk runs the design live. Each month it nominates 20 pairs and holds them for six months, as in the paper. Its screen lists every nominated pair still inside its trading period.
screens.question: In month 30, how many nominated pairs are on the screen?

hints.text: How many portfolios are live in month 30?
From month 5 on, six portfolios overlap.

feedback.correct: Correct. Six overlapping portfolios of 20 pairs.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Count the live portfolios, then the pairs in each.

byKey.one: 20 is one portfolio. Five older ones are still trading.
byKey.legs: 240 counts each leg. The screen lists pairs.

explain.text: Six portfolios overlap, so the screen holds 6 × 20 = 120 pairs. A share can appear in several of them. Most will be waiting for a 2 sd gap.

ideas: Form pairs over 12 months, then trade them over the next 6.
Everything that chooses or measures, including the 2 sd trigger, is fixed at the end of formation.
A new portfolio starts each month, so six trade at once.

formula.name: One cycle
formula.note: Formation, then trading, in trading days.

summary.trap: Measuring the sd on the trading period uses prices the desk has not seen yet.

quiz.prose: A backtest computes each pair's spread sd from the six trading months, then opens at 2 sd.
quiz.question: What is wrong?

options.text: It uses future prices to set today's threshold
Six months is too few days
options.why: The number of days is not the problem. Their dates are.

options.text: Nothing, the sd is the same either way
options.why: It differs: here 0.0300 against 0.0210, and it uses the future.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Ask which prices exist on the first trading day.

explain.text: The threshold must be known before trading starts. The trading-period sd needs the period's last price.

quiz.prose: Portfolios are named by their first trading month, from month 0, and each trades for 6 months.
quiz.question: How many portfolios trade in month 2?

feedback.generic: Not quite. Count only portfolios that already exist.

byKey.six: Six overlap only from month 5. In month 2 only three exist.

explain.text: Months 0, 1 and 2 have each started one portfolio, so 3 trade. All three are still within their six months.

quiz.prose: Five rules of the design are listed.
quiz.question: Which one belongs to the trading period?

options.text: Close a pair when the prices cross

options.why: Scaling is done once, at the start of formation.
Ranking chooses pairs, so it uses formation data.
The sd is fixed at the end of formation.

feedback.correct: Correct. Closing acts on a trading day.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Trading rules act on a day; formation rules choose or measure.

explain.text: Closing at a crossing reads each trading day's prices. The other three are fixed before trading starts.
